title: The Heat Kernel Expansion: Curvature for Shock Detection in Higher-Order Financial Networks
abstract: This work follows the evolution of financial networks in Norway over a period of nine years at a monthly rate. The data consist of board directors and their affiliations to companies, which we model as simplicial complexes. In this framework, directors are represented as nodes and companies as faces of the complex. To characterize the latter, we focus on three topological measures: the Euler characteristic, computed through the Betti numbers, torsion computed through the reduced determinant of the higher-order Laplacians, and higher-order clustering coefficients. The first two fail to capture the effect of imposed law on representation, unlike our notion of curvature which is a geometrical measure computed from the coefficients of the series expansion of the heat kernel in powers of time, which is our major contribution in this work. In particular, the Euler characteristic integrates curvature, and thus local information is lost. Subsequently, not every topological measure can reliably capture shocks in networks. Further, the number of spanning trees may undergo significant changes at the lowest order, yet these changes need not be reflected in the torsion. Conversely, the change in the curvature revealed variation in the board interlock due to legislation, and serves as a sensitive measure for detecting shocks in networks. Inflection points in curvature are associated with external forcing, and minima with shock arrival times. Sharp transitions are also observed in the components of torsion, while smooth changes are observed in higher-order clustering.
summary: This work applies advanced algebraic topology and geometric analysis to model financial networks as simplicial complexes. The core contribution is using curvature, derived from the heat kernel expansion, as a superior diagnostic tool for detecting structural shocks caused by external laws compared to traditional measures like Euler characteristic or torsion. It demonstrates that this geometric approach accurately pinpoints the timing of regulatory impacts on network structure.
main_problem: To develop a robust geometric measure, derived from the heat kernel expansion, capable of detecting structural shocks in high-order financial networks, surpassing the limitations of traditional topological invariants.
main_result: Curvature dynamics provide a sensitive indicator for external forcing or legislative changes (shocks), showing distinct features like inflection points and minima that raw network counts fail to capture.
method: The authors employ algebraic topology on simplicial complexes, calculating curvature via the heat kernel expansion of higher-order Laplacians. This geometric measure is compared against standard topological tools like Betti numbers and torsion.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a financial network in Norway over nine years, represented as a simplicial complex where directors are nodes and company affiliations form faces (simplices).
key_observables: Curvature ($ ar{R}(t)$), Euler characteristic ($\chi$), Reidemeister torsion ($	au_R$), and higher-order clustering coefficients ($ ar{C}_k(t)$).
important_parameters: Time ($t$) evolution, network order (dimension of the complex), and specific external forcing events (e.g., legislation dates).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that geometric curvature derived from the heat kernel expansion retains local information about structural changes better than integrated topological measures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temporal evolution of curvature ($ ar{R}(t)$) showing shock markers coinciding with legislation dates, alongside comparisons of $\chi$, torsion, and higher-order clustering coefficients for male/female groups.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of standard topological measures (Euler characteristic loses local info; torsion is insensitive). It then introduces curvature from the heat kernel expansion as a superior geometric invariant. Finally, it applies this method to analyze real-world financial data, demonstrating its predictive power regarding external shocks.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the methodology—using spectral geometry (heat kernel) on high-order complexes to detect non-equilibrium structural changes—is conceptually transferable to analyzing phase transitions or sudden regime shifts in complex quantum many-body systems.
